text.p: The contentious measures from the Australian government's August budget are expected to appear in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, in the next few weeks, government representatives told Reuters on Friday.

Once the Senate has finished with bills relating to labour reform and the partial sale of state-owned telecoms carrier Telstra Corp (see accompanying report), the way will be clear for the remaining budget measures to move into the final stages of the parliamentary process.
The contentious budget bills -- those containing measures that may be opposed by both the Labor opposition and the Australian Democrats -- are detailed here:
HIGHER EDUCATION CONTRIBUTION SCHEME AMENDMENT BILL, 1996
This bill is currently in the lower house of parliament, the House of Representatives, still at an early stage of processing. It is expected to be debated in the Senate later this month.
It includes:
-- Student charges. The government wants to hike the charges for some university courses for new students. Value to the budget: A$66 million in 1997/98, A$123 million in 1999/00.

-- Student charges repayments. Students can defer payment of their charges until their income reaches a certain threshold. The government wants to drop that threshold, initiating faster repayments. Value: A$230 million in 1997/98, A$318 million in 1999/00.
-- Student income support ("Austudy"). The government wants to tighten eligibility, in part by commencing eligibility at a greater age. Value: A$63 million in 1997/98, A$78 million in 1999/00.
CHILDCARE LEGISLATION AMENDMENT BILL, 1996

The House of Representatives passed this bill about two weeks ago and it is likely to move into the Senate before the end of the year. The Australian Democrats said earlier in the year they were open to negotiation on this bill.

"Until the legislation is debated, who knows what the Democrats are going to do, but we've held talks and we're hopeful that the legislation will be supported," a spokeswoman for Family Services Minister Judi Moylan told Reuters.
The contentious measure in the bill is a tightening of eligibility for childcare subsidies. Value: A$147 million in 1997/98, A$170 million in 1999/00.
TAXATION LAWS AMENDMENT BILL (NO.3) 1996
The House of Representatives is expected to debate this bill next week. It is expected in the Senate before the end of the year.
It includes:

-- Research and development tax break legislation. Companies can deduct 150 percent of R&D spending from taxable income. The government wants to cut this to 125 percent. Value: A$430 million in 1997/98, A$440 million in 1999/00.

-- Medical expenses rebate. People whose medical expenses exceed A$1,000 a year get a tax rebate, depending on their income. The government wants to raise the income threshold. Value: A$26 million in 1997/98, A$24 million in 1999/00.
NATIONAL HEALTH BUDGET MEASURES BILL 1996

This bill has passed through the House of Representatives but has not been introduced into the Senate. Health Minister Michael Wooldridge's office expects it to be dealt with sooner rather than later.
It contains pharmaceutical benefit scheme changes. The government wants people to pay more for each prescription. Value: A$134 million in 1997/98, A$147 million in 1999/00.
OTHER MEASURES
The government's aged care legislation has not been introduced into the lower house and is unlikely to be this year, so there is no bill yet.

The legislation will include contentious nursing home changes. The government wants residents to pay more, as they do in other forms of accommodation for the aged. Value: A$125 million in 1997/98, A$194 million in 1999/00.
Also, changes to court fees were effected by regulation, not legislation. The Senate, using its power to alter any regulation, imposed some minor amendments in early October.
Before amendment, the measure was expected to raise less than A$27 million in 1997/98 and something under A$31 million in 1999/00.
